issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s surrender of a building under compulsion of a requisition order is vacation for sufficient cause and does not trigger the statutory restriction on seeking possession for personal occupation.
material_facts: The landlord occupied part of a house, while another part was let to a judge.
A competent authority requisitioned the entire house for the judge’s occupation.
After surrendering the house, the landlord sought possession of another building from its tenant for his own occupation.
issues.conclusion: Surrendering the building in compliance with the requisition order was for sufficient cause, so the restriction in the second proviso to Section 14(3) did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(3) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, permits an application for possession for the landlord’s own occupation, subject to the second proviso. “Sufficient cause” is construed liberally according to its ordinary meaning of an adequate or enough justifiable reason; a genuine, bona fide reason is sufficient. A landlord compelled by a competent authority’s requisition order to vacate has sufficient cause. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.landlord_own_occupation_eviction_applica: A landlord applied to recover a building from a tenant for the landlord’s own occupation.
predicates.building_surrendered_under_requisition_o: The landlord gave up possession of a building because a competent authority requisitioned it.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeking possession for personal occupation surrendered a building because it was requisitioned by a competent authority, the surrender counts as sufficient cause.

issues.legal_issue: The validity of a requisition order and the landlord’s failure to object to it cannot be used to deny that surrendering the building was for sufficient cause.
material_facts: The landlord did not object to the requisition proceedings.
The lower courts treated the absence of an objection as a reason to regard the requisition as improperly made and to find insufficient cause for the landlord’s surrender.
The landlord’s application for possession was considered under rent-control law, while the requisition was made under separate legislation.
issues.conclusion: Whether the requisition order was valid or invalid, and whether the landlord objected to it, could not adversely affect the sufficiency of the cause for surrender; rent-control authorities could not examine the order’s merits.
issues.legal_principle: The Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, and the Himachal Pradesh Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1972, address different matters. Under Section 14(3)’s second proviso, the sufficiency of the cause for vacating is not determined by the validity of a requisition order. Even surrender under an incorrect order of a competent authority is for sufficient cause, and rent-control authorities cannot review the merits of that order. The landlord’s failure to object does not alter that principle. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.landlord_own_occupation_eviction_applica: A landlord applied to recover a building from a tenant for the landlord’s own occupation.
predicates.competent_authority_issued_requisition_o: A competent authority made an order requiring the building to be made available for another person’s occupation.
predicates.landlord_surrendered_building_under_that: The landlord gave up possession of the building in response to the authority’s order.

issues.definition: If a landlord seeking personal occupation surrendered a building in response to a competent authority’s requisition, the order’s validity and the landlord’s failure to object do not negate sufficient cause.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s wealth or the possibility of occasional use of a building does not, without more, defeat the landlord’s claim to possession for personal occupation.
material_facts: The landlord had no other building in the urban area concerned.
The landlord had vacated another building for sufficient cause after it was requisitioned.
The lower courts inferred that the landlord would not occupy the building or would use it only occasionally because he was wealthy.
issues.conclusion: The wealth-based inference was not well founded; because the landlord had no other building and had vacated the other building for sufficient cause, there was no fetter on his right to seek possession for his own occupation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(3)(a)(i) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, allows a landlord to seek possession of a residential building for the landlord’s own occupation, subject to the statutory conditions, including that the landlord is not occupying another residential building owned by him in the urban area. The second proviso does not bar the claim where the landlord vacated the other building for sufficient cause. The judgment rejects wealth or presumed occasional use as a sufficient basis for denying the claim on these facts. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.landlord_own_occupation_eviction_applica: A landlord applied to recover a residential building from a tenant for the landlord’s own occupation.
predicates.no_other_owned_residential_building_in_u: The landlord owned no other residential building in the relevant urban area.
predicates.other_building_vacated_for_sufficient_ca: The landlord had vacated another building for a genuine and justifiable reason.
predicates.lower_court_relied_on_wealth_or_occasion: A lower court inferred from the landlord’s wealth or possible occasional use that the landlord would not occupy the building.

issues.definition: Where a landlord seeking personal occupation has no other owned residential building in the area and vacated another building for sufficient cause, an inference based on wealth or possible occasional use does not defeat the claim.
